title: After the outage, what do you actually fix?
summary: A nine-hour outage produced fourteen action items and a leadership expectation that all of them happen. Decide what genuinely reduces risk.

brief.role: You are the PM for the platform team.
brief.company: Northvale, a 300-person company selling appointment software to healthcare clinics.
brief.context: Last Tuesday a database migration locked a table for nine hours during business hours. Clinics could not book or check in patients. 1,900 clinics were affected. The postmortem produced fourteen action items and the COO has told the executive team that 'we are fixing all of them'. Your engineering lead says the fourteen would take about two quarters. You own the plan and present it Friday.
brief.objective: Reduce the chance and the cost of a repeat, honestly, within a defensible amount of work.
brief.constraints: Six engineers. You have roughly one quarter before other committed work resumes. Two of the fourteen items are already in progress.
brief.task: Decide which items you commit to and how you present the rest.

evidenceCards.title: Incident timeline
evidenceCards.content:
09:12 — Migration runs. It adds a column with a default value, which locks the appointments table on this database version.
09:14 — Error rates spike. Automated alert fires to the on-call channel.
09:31 — On-call engineer acknowledges. (Alert routing sent it to a channel, not a page; the engineer was in a meeting.)
09:48 — Cause identified as the migration.
10:05 — Attempt to cancel the migration fails; the operation is not safely cancellable partway.
10:20 — Decision to wait it out rather than fail over, based on an estimate that the migration would complete 'soon'.
13:40 — Escalated to the head of infrastructure, who begins preparing a failover.
16:30 — Failover to the replica completes. Service restored.
17:05 — Status page updated for the first time. Support had been answering individually for seven hours.

Breakdown of the nine hours: 19 minutes to detect and acknowledge, 36 minutes to diagnose, 6h 25m in the 'wait it out' decision, 2h 50m to execute the failover.

evidenceCards.title: The fourteen action items
evidenceCards.content:
With engineering estimates in engineer-weeks:

1. Migrations require review by a second engineer — 0.5 (in progress)
2. Lint rule blocking lock-taking migration patterns on this DB version — 1
3. Migrations run in a maintenance window, not business hours — 0.5
4. Alerts page a human rather than post to a channel — 0.5
5. Documented failover runbook with a practised drill — 3
6. Automated status page updates driven by error-rate thresholds — 2
7. Reduce failover time from 2h 50m to under 30 minutes — 8
8. Read replica in a second region — 12
9. Blue-green deployment for schema changes — 14
10. Incident commander role and rotation — 1 (in progress)
11. Customer comms templates pre-approved by legal — 1
12. Per-clinic offline booking mode in the client apps — 16
13. Chaos testing programme — 6
14. Migration rollback tooling — 5

Total: roughly 70 engineer-weeks. Team capacity for the quarter: about 72 engineer-weeks, minus the 20% the team already spends on support and maintenance.

evidenceCards.title: Risk and history analysis
evidenceCards.content:
Migrations run roughly 40 times a quarter. Reviewing the last two years:
- 3 migrations caused customer-visible degradation. All 3 were lock-taking patterns that item 2's lint rule would have caught.
- 0 incidents in two years were caused by a regional failure, which item 8 addresses.
- 4 incidents in two years exceeded one hour. In all 4, the largest time block was decision-making, not execution.

Support data from this incident: 1,240 inbound contacts. The support lead estimates 70% would have been avoided by a status page updated at 09:30.

Customer impact: 6 clinics have asked for contractual uptime commitments since. Two mentioned the seven-hour communications gap specifically and neither mentioned the technical cause.

The head of infrastructure's note: 'Items 8, 9 and 12 are good engineering. None of them would have shortened Tuesday. What shortened Tuesday would have been paging someone, having a runbook, and someone with authority to call failover at 10:20 instead of 13:40.'

evidenceCards.title: Expectations around the plan
evidenceCards.content:
COO, in the executive meeting: 'We are fixing all fourteen.' In a follow-up conversation with you: 'What I need is to tell the board this cannot happen again, and to tell the six clinics asking for SLAs something credible.'

Engineering lead: 'If I commit to all fourteen, I will deliver about nine of them badly and the team will spend the quarter context-switching. I would rather commit to six and finish them.'

Support lead: 'Whatever else you do, please do the status page one. I had seven hours of people asking me the same question and nothing to point them at.'

Head of product: 'Other committed work resumes next quarter regardless. Do not build a plan that assumes it will not.'

None of the six clinics asking for SLAs has threatened to leave. Two are in the top 50 accounts.

decisionPrompt: Which of the fourteen items do you commit to this quarter, and how do you handle the expectation that all fourteen happen?

decisionOptions.label: Commit to the prevention, response and communication items; schedule the rest explicitly
decisionOptions.description: Take items 1-6, 10, 11 and 14 — roughly 14 engineer-weeks — finish them properly, and present the remaining five as a dated, costed backlog with the risk each one addresses.
decisionOptions.consequence:
All nine ship within seven weeks. The lint rule catches two lock-taking migrations in the first quarter. A drill in week five exposes a gap in the runbook that is fixed before it matters.
The COO is initially unhappy with 'nine of fourteen' and satisfied once you show that the five deferred items would not have shortened Tuesday, with the head of infrastructure's note behind it. The board framing becomes 'the failure mode that caused this is now blocked, and our response time is 20 minutes instead of seven hours', which survives scrutiny.
The six clinics get a written reliability commitment; four are satisfied, two continue to push for contractual SLAs, which commercial handles separately.
The team has 45 engineer-weeks left, which absorbs the support load and starts the deferred work early.
Trade-off: you did not do what the COO announced, and you spent political effort making the case for a smaller, finished plan.
decisionOptions.rubricNote: Strongest when the rationale uses the time breakdown (6h25m in decision-making), the history (all 3 prior migration incidents were the same pattern), and separates what would have shortened Tuesday from good engineering that would not.

decisionOptions.label: Commit to all fourteen
decisionOptions.description: The COO has already announced it. Commit the quarter and most of the next to the full list.
decisionOptions.consequence:
By the end of the quarter, four items are complete, five are partially done, and five have not started. The lint rule — one engineer-week and the single highest-value item — is among the partially done, because it was scheduled after the regional replica work.
In week nine another lock-taking migration reaches production. It is caught in review, by luck, by the second reviewer from item 1.
The next quarter's committed work starts late. The COO's board statement has to be softened.
Trade-off: you matched the announcement and delivered less actual risk reduction than a third of the work would have.
decisionOptions.rubricNote: Weak. The engineering lead predicted this outcome explicitly, and the sequencing failure is the specific cost of committing to everything.

decisionOptions.label: Prioritise the structural engineering items
decisionOptions.description: Take items 7, 8, 9 and 12 — the ones that address the architecture — on the grounds that process fixes do not prevent the next different failure.
decisionOptions.consequence:
Two of the four complete in the quarter; the blue-green schema work slips into the next.
The architecture is genuinely better. In month two a migration with the same lock-taking pattern reaches production, is not caught because the lint rule was not built, and causes a 40-minute degradation. It is shorter than Tuesday only because someone happened to be watching.
The status page is still manual. Support absorbs another day of individual replies.
Trade-off: you invested in durable structural improvement and left the cheap, specific, historically-validated fixes undone.
decisionOptions.rubricNote: Low. The history says 3 of 3 migration incidents share one pattern that a one-week lint rule blocks. Ignoring the cheapest highest-frequency fix for architecture is the core error.

decisionOptions.label: Focus on detection and communication
decisionOptions.description: Take items 4, 5, 6, 10 and 11 — paging, runbook, status page, incident commander, comms templates — on the grounds that the nine hours were a response failure, not a migration failure.
decisionOptions.consequence:
All five ship in five weeks and they work: a subsequent incident is detected in 3 minutes, communicated in 12, and resolved in 50.
But the incident happens, because nothing was done about the migration pattern that caused it. The lint rule was one engineer-week and was not in the plan.
The COO asks, reasonably, why a fix costing one week for a failure mode that has occurred three times in two years was not included.
Trade-off: you correctly identified that most of the nine hours was response, and left the cause unaddressed.
decisionOptions.rubricNote: Good diagnosis of where the time went, incomplete conclusion. Credit the time-breakdown reasoning; mark down for omitting the cheapest prevention item with the strongest historical support.

rubric.referenceReasoning: The timeline decomposes the nine hours: 19 minutes to detect, 36 to diagnose, 6h25m stuck in a decision, and 2h50m executing. So the dominant cost was neither the migration nor the failover speed — it was that nobody had the runbook, the authority or the practice to call failover at 10:20. Separately, the history says every one of the three migration incidents in two years shared one pattern that a one-engineer-week lint rule would block, while zero incidents in two years came from the regional failure that item 8 addresses. And the customer evidence points at communication: 70% of 1,240 contacts avoidable with a status page, and the two clinics that complained specifically cited the comms gap rather than the outage. Those three readings converge on the cheap items — prevention, paging, runbook, incident command, status page, rollback tooling — totalling around 14 engineer-weeks. The structural items are good engineering that would not have shortened Tuesday, which is exactly how they should be presented rather than quietly dropped.
evidenceSignals: Decomposes the nine hours and finds 6h25m in decision-making
Notes all 3 prior migration incidents share the pattern the 1-week lint rule blocks
Notes zero incidents in two years came from regional failure
Uses the 70%-of-contacts figure to value the status page item
Notices the complaining clinics cited the comms gap, not the technical cause
Uses the head of infrastructure's assessment of which items would have shortened Tuesday

product_sense: Distinguishes reducing incident probability from reducing incident cost and covers both
analytics: Uses incident history to weight items by observed frequency rather than by severity of imagination
Sizes the support impact of the communication gap
user_research: Notices what customers actually complained about differs from what engineering focused on
prioritization: Ranks by risk reduced per engineer-week rather than by how substantial an item sounds
Leaves capacity for the 20% support load and next quarter's committed work
execution: Prefers finishing nine items to starting fourteen
Includes a drill so the runbook is tested rather than written
Keeps the two in-progress items rather than restarting the plan
communication: Gives the COO a board-credible sentence rather than a count of items
Presents deferred items with their dates and the specific risk each addresses
Answers the six clinics with something specific rather than a promise of everything

product_sense: Treats the postmortem list as a specification rather than a set of candidate risk reductions
analytics: Ignores that the same migration pattern caused all three prior incidents
Weights the regional replica highly despite zero occurrences in two years
prioritization: Commits to all fourteen after being told it produces nine done badly
Skips the one-week lint rule while funding twelve-week architecture work
execution: Writes a runbook without a drill
Plans the full quarter with no allowance for the team's existing support load
communication: Silently drops items rather than presenting them as dated and costed
Leaves the COO's public commitment unaddressed

learnTakeaway.title: Postmortem lists are candidates, not commitments
learnTakeaway.body: A postmortem generates every action someone could imagine, which is the right output for that meeting and the wrong input for a plan. Turning it into work means asking two questions of each item: how much of this specific incident would it have removed, and how often has the risk it addresses actually occurred. Those two questions usually promote a handful of cheap process and communication fixes above the architectural items, and they give you the language to defer the rest visibly instead of silently.

qaSubmissions.label: strong
qaSubmissions.rationale: Decomposing the nine hours changes the list: 19 minutes to detect, 36 to diagnose, 2h50m executing — and 6h25m was one unmade decision. So the highest-value work is making the call happen: paging, a drilled runbook, an incident commander. On cause, all three migration incidents in two years share the pattern item 2 blocks for one engineer-week; item 8 addresses a failure that's happened zero times. Customers cited the seven-hour silence, not the database. I'd commit 1-6, 10, 11 and 14, and hand the COO the other five dated and costed rather than dropped quietly.

qaSubmissions.label: defensible_alternative
qaSubmissions.rationale: I'd commit to 4, 5, 6, 10 and 11 — paging, runbook and drill, automated status page, incident commander, pre-approved comms — about 7.5 engineer-weeks, finished in five. The timeline is unambiguous: 6h25m of nine hours was a decision nobody was empowered to make. Prevention only ever addresses the failure mode that already happened; response capability shortens every incident, including the one we haven't imagined. Where this is weak: item 2 is one engineer-week and would have caught all three migration incidents. I'd add it if I have any room.

qaSubmissions.label: weak
qaSubmissions.rationale: The postmortem identified fourteen real problems and the COO has already told the executive team we are fixing all of them. The total is about 70 engineer-weeks against 72 of capacity, so it fits. I would commit to all fourteen and sequence the biggest ones first since they take longest.
